prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

I wonder, by my troth, what thou and I Did, till we loved? Were we not weaned till then? But sucked on country pleasures, childishly? Or snorted we in the Seven Sleepers’ den? ’Twas so; but this, all pleasures fancies be. If ever any beauty I did see, Which I desired, and got, ’twas but a dream of thee. And now good-morrow to our waking souls, Which watch not one another out of fear; For love, all love of other sights controls, And makes one little room an everywhere. Let sea-discoverers to new worlds have gone, Let maps to other, worlds on worlds have shown, Let us possess one world, each hath one, and is one. My face in thine eye, thine in mine appears, And true plain hearts do in the faces rest; Where can we find two better hemispheres, Without sharp north, without declining west? Whatever dies, was not mixed equally; If our two loves be one, or, thou and I Love so alike, that none do slacken, none can die.

- The speaker views life before true love as childish, unconscious, and filled with merely imagined pleasures.
- Any previous beauty the speaker desired now seems like only a dream or foreshadowing of the beloved.
- Their awakened love is free from fear and makes their small shared space feel as vast as the entire world.
- The lovers see themselves reflected in each other, forming two perfectly balanced and harmonious halves.

prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: Did, Were, But

outputs.L1:
I wonder, by my troth, what thou and I  
Did till we loved. Were we not weaned till then,  
But childishly sucked on country pleasures?  
Or snorted we in the Seven Sleepers’ den?  
’Twas so; but this—all pleasures fancies be.  
If ever any beauty I did see,  
Which I desired and got, ’twas but a dream of thee.

And now, good morrow to our waking souls,  
Which watch not one another out of fear;  
For love all love of other sights controls,  
And makes one little room an everywhere.  
Let sea-discoverers to new worlds have gone;  
Let maps to others worlds on worlds have shown;  
Let us possess one world: each hath one, and is one.

My face in thine eye, thine in mine, appears,  
And true, plain hearts do in the faces rest.  
Where can we find two better hemispheres,  
Without sharp north, without declining west?  
Whatever dies was not mixed equally.  
If our two loves be one, or thou and I  
Love so alike that none do slacken, none can die.
outputs.L2:
Honestly, what were you and I doing before we fell in love? Had we not yet grown beyond infancy, feeding naïvely on simple, rustic pleasures? Or were we asleep in the cave of the Seven Sleepers? Surely we were, because every pleasure we knew then was only an illusion. Any beautiful person I ever saw, wanted, and possessed was merely a shadowy foretelling of you.

Now, let us greet the morning of our awakened souls. We no longer watch each other with suspicion, because our love makes every other sight unimportant and transforms this small room into an entire universe. Let explorers sail away to discover new lands, and let maps reveal world after world to others. We will hold one world between us: each of us possesses a world and is one.

My face is reflected in your eyes, just as yours is reflected in mine, and our sincere hearts can be seen plainly in our faces. Where could we discover two finer hemispheres, with neither a freezing north nor a west where the sun declines? Anything that dies was made from elements combined in unequal proportions. But if our two loves are truly one—or if you and I love with such perfect equality that neither love can weaken—then neither love can ever die.
outputs.L3:
The speaker looks back on life before experiencing true love as a period of childishness and unconsciousness. The pleasures once enjoyed now seem insubstantial, as though they were merely imagined rather than fully real. Likewise, every beautiful person or object the speaker previously desired appears in retrospect to have been only a dream or a faint foreshadowing of the beloved.

With the awakening of genuine love, the speaker enters a new and more meaningful existence. This love is secure and free from fear, allowing the lovers to find an entire world within their small shared space. They no longer need adventure or distant places because their devotion gives their immediate surroundings a sense of boundless richness.

As the lovers gaze at one another, each sees their own image reflected in the other’s eyes. This mutual reflection suggests that they are two equal, perfectly balanced halves of a single harmonious whole. Neither person’s love is lesser or incomplete. Because their affection is unified and equally shared, the speaker believes it cannot diminish, weaken, or die.
outputs.L4:
The speaker begins by wondering what he and his beloved did before they fell in love. He asks whether their earlier lives were childish, almost as if they had been asleep or confined to a nursery. Any pleasures they experienced before meeting now seem unreal and insignificant; if the speaker ever thought he loved someone else, those experiences were merely dreams or imperfect anticipations of his present beloved.

Their mutual love has awakened them into a new life, like souls greeting a “good morrow.” Because they are completely absorbed in one another, they no longer need to seek adventure or distraction elsewhere. Explorers may travel across oceans and map new worlds, but the lovers possess an entire world within their shared space. Each sees a world reflected in the other’s face and eyes, so that their two individual worlds become one.

The speaker finally compares their love to two hemispheres joined into a perfect globe. Unlike the physical hemispheres of the earth, their world has no cold north and no declining west, images associated with decay and death. Their love is equally shared and perfectly balanced: neither person loves less than the other. Because their love is unified and free from inequality, the speaker suggests that it cannot weaken or die.
outputs.L5: Yesterday, we **did** something special. We visited a small village where the streets **were** quiet and the houses were colorful. We wanted to stay longer, **but** it started to rain. Although the weather changed, we did not feel disappointed because the people were friendly and the trip was unforgettable.
